newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Norway seeks more EU talks to settle salmon row.
newsitem.headline: Norway seeks more EU talks to settle salmon row.

text.p: Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal on Monday called for further talks with the European Union to settle a row over trade in farmed salmon.

The EU executive is considering an average duty of 13.7 percent on imports of Norwegian salmon, accusing Norwegian producers of receiving state subsidies and dumping the fish on the EU market at less than the cost of production.
"It's an issue which should be solved between good neighbours, not hostile third parties," Godal told a news conference after talks with EU External Affairs Commissioner Hans van den Broek.
Norway, like the EU, is a member of the 18-nation European Economic Area but its voters rejected EU membership in a 1994 referendum.

Godal, who is also due to discuss the issue with EU External Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan on Wednesday, said that he had never seen the EU take such a "confrontational" measure when the problem could be resolved through talks.
"It would be prohibitive. We would be out of the market," he said, referring to the duty envisaged in a confidential European Commission report recently leaked to the media.

Norwegian Fisheries Minister Karl Eirik Schuett-Pedersen told the news conference that European consumers and the fish processing industry would be hit by higher prices if Norwegian salmon was kept out.
Norwegian salmon exports were worth seven billion Norwegian crowns a year ($1.0 billion) and 97 percent of processed salmon was exported.
If not Norwegians would have to eat half a tonne of salmon each annually, Schuett-Pedersen added.
On Monday, several member states, notably Sweden and Denmark told a meeting of the EU anti-dumping committee that further negotiations should be held with Norway, EU sources said.
Other member states said during a long discussion they needed more time to study the confidential report of the European Commission and were given until next week to express their views.
But Britain and Ireland pressed strongly for the EU to curb imports of Norwegian salmon, other EU sources said.
The Commission is due to decide by the end of May whether to impose provisional import duties for six months and may take into account the opinions of member states before taking a final decision.
In September, the Commission said it was looking into Scottish complaints that imports of salmon from Norway were being subsidised and dumped, depressing prices and hurting the EU industry.
